newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bourse rebounds, but storm clouds linger.
newsitem.headline: Thai bourse rebounds, but storm clouds linger.

text.p: Thailand's stock market recouped losses for the second day in a row on Monday as nervous investors took solace in government moves to solve a crisis over cash-strapped finance companies and the slowing economy.
But analysts warned that storm clouds would continue to hang over the country's financial markets until proposed measures for the finance sector became concrete.

"I think it's too early to say the crisis is over," said Graham Catterwell, head of equities at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "A lot of finance companies are going to have to raise capital. A lot won't be able to, and then the question is -- what happens then?"

Bargain-hunters snapped up cheap finance and banking stocks on Monday, driving the SET index up more than 2.7 percent at one stage. It closed above the crucial 700-point level at 703.32, up 11.87, or 1.72 percent.

The index fell almost five percent last week as nervous investors made hefty deposit withdrawals from ailing finance firms, which have been hit hard by high interest rates and a four-year-old slump in the property market.

The central bank's statement on Friday it would guarantee repayment of promissory notes issued by finance companies put a brake on the deposits run -- but not before a massive 15-20 billion baht ($578-770 million) had been withdrawn.
The baht, which the government has doggedly defended against speculators with a tight monetary stance, ended little changed on Monday around 25.937/25.942 to the dollar.
In a dramatic shake-up last week, Thai authorities ordered 10 finance firms, hard-hit by a liquidity crunch, to raise capital by a total of 8.25 billion baht.

They also told banks and finance companies to raise provisions for sub-standard assets, primarily to the property sector, by 15 percent and 20 percent respectively on top of the 100 percent required for bad and doubtful loans.

The government followed up its bitter-pill prescriptions with a scheme to raise up to 100 billion baht through zero-coupon bonds to take troubled property assets off the finance firms' balance sheets. Cabinet approval for the plan will be sought on Tuesday.
"All this is just talk," said one analyst at a Thai finance security firm. "There's been nothing concrete yet... If there has been any change, there has been a change in sentiment."

Analysts said the finance sector faced a long slog to cure its ills. Many would face a slide in profitability after years of plenty, many would be forced to merge and some would probably go to the wall.

"It wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing if some of them went down," said one analyst at a foreign bank, who declined to be identified. "This time the government seems to be saying 'you're on your own, guys' and taking the view that the system is strong enough to take it on the chin."
Central bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Saturday that a "carrot and stick" approach would be used to encourage mergers among the country's 91 financial firms.
His call was backed by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, who was quoted in the headline of the daily Bangkok Post on Monday as telling the finance firms to "shape up or ship out". (US$1 = 25.9 baht)
